# Where can I get historical Treasury futures data?

Short answer: FinzData sells historical Treasury futures data, including 10-year Treasury note futures (ZN): every contract since 2007 with 1-minute, 5-minute, 15-minute, 30-minute, hourly and daily bars, open interest by contract and continuous series, as CSV, REST API or MCP. The full ZN history is a one-time $39 at finzdata.com/shop.

## What the Treasury futures data covers

FinzData covers 10-year Treasury note futures (ZN) as part of 139 futures markets, each with every contract since 2007, not just a stitched front month. See the market page at finzdata.com/futures/zn and the full list at finzdata.com/futures-data.

  * Bars at 1-minute, 5-minute, 15-minute, 30-minute, hourly and daily.
  * Open interest by contract, so you can see where positions sit across the curve and through each roll.
  * Continuous series built from every contract, with the roll dates kept.

This is the historical data rates traders need to study yield moves, roll behaviour and positioning around Fed meetings and economic releases.

## How to get it: CSV, API and MCP

FinzData delivers every dataset three ways, so it fits any workflow:

  * CSV downloads: one file per contract and bar size, ready for pandas, R, Excel or a backtesting engine.
  * REST API at `https://api.finzdata.com`: query by symbol, contract and date range from Python or any language.
  * MCP server at `https://api.finzdata.com/mcp`: ChatGPT, Claude and other AI agents can pull the data and run server-side backtests directly.

## Why every contract matters for rates backtests

A backtest on a single back-adjusted series can hide the cost and timing of real rolls. With every individual contract you trade the instruments that actually existed on each day, see the roll from one quarter to the next, and measure liquidity from the real volume and open interest. Pair Treasury futures with the 18,000+ macro series FinzData keeps with every vintage, so rate and inflation signals only use what was known on the day, with no look-ahead bias.

## What it costs and what is free

The full history of one futures market is a one-time purchase of $39 at finzdata.com/shop: you pay once and keep the files. Daily updates are optional and can be removed at checkout.

A free API key needs just an email at finzdata.com. It covers the last 30 days of futures and daily GEX, plus the last 12 months of daily US stock bars, COT, SEC fundamentals, macro series and 13F holdings, with 1,000 data calls a day. Try the API with your own code before you buy.

## Questions

Where can I download historical 10-year Treasury futures data?

FinzData sells the full ZN history, every contract since 2007 with intraday and daily bars and open interest, as CSV, REST API or MCP for a one-time $39.

Does the Treasury futures data include open interest?

Yes. Open interest comes by contract for every ZN contract, alongside volume and OHLC bars.

Is there 1-minute Treasury futures data?

Yes. ZN comes with 1-minute, 5-minute, 15-minute, 30-minute, hourly and daily bars for every contract since 2007.

Can I get Treasury futures data as a CSV file?

Yes. Every contract and bar size downloads as CSV, and the same data is available through the REST API and the MCP server.

Can I try it before I buy?

Yes. A free API key with just an email gives the last 30 days of futures data and 1,000 calls a day.

# Forecasting Bond Returns Using Jumps in Intraday Prices

Journal of Fixed Income, Vol. 20, No. 4, 2011

19 Pages Posted: 1 Dec 2010 Last revised: 4 Apr 2013

## Johan G. Duyvesteyn

Robeco Institutional Asset Management

## Martin Martens

Robeco Institutional Asset Management

## Siawash Safavi Nic

Robeco Institutional Asset Management

Date Written: November 28, 2010

### Abstract

We build on the work of Wright and Zhou (2009) who show that the average jump mean in bond prices can predict excess bond returns, capturing the countercyclical behaviour of risk premia. We show that these jumps often take place at 8:30 and 10:00 directly linking them to specific macroeconomic news announcements. Mean-reversion, which looks at the total return over the past period rather than just the part related to jumps, has no predictive ability. Hence it is important to consider excess returns that are related to macroeconomic announcements that matter to market participants, and jumps are a good market proxy for what investors believe is important news. Our improved jump measure produces a Sharpe ratio of 0.52 in an out-of-sample market-neutral investment strategy.

Keywords: Bond return predictability, mean-reversion, realized jumps

License Information

The copyright holder has granted SSRN a license. All rights reserved. No reuse allowed without permission.

JEL Classification: E37, G14

Suggested Citation

Duyvesteyn, Johan G. and Martens, Martin P.E. and Safavi Nic, Siawash, Forecasting Bond Returns Using Jumps in Intraday Prices (November 28, 2010). Journal of Fixed Income, Vol. 20, No. 4, 2011, Available at SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1716759 or http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.1716759

# Historical Futures Data: Daily, Intraday and Continuous Contracts

Historical futures data for 139 markets — equity index, rates, energy, metals, grains, softs, livestock, currencies, volatility and crypto — from CME, CBOT, NYMEX, COMEX, ICE, Eurex and Cboe. More than 17,500 individual contracts since 2007, a roll calendar, and back-adjusted continuous series, as CSV, JSON or Parquet through one API and a Python client.

Free tier: the last 12 months of daily futures bars, 1,000 calls/day, no card required.

## Historical futures data coverage: daily and intraday

Data  | Coverage  | Detail  | Plan
--- | --- | --- | ---
Daily bars, every contract  | 139 markets, 17,500+ contracts, 2007 to today  | Open, high, low, close, volume, open interest  | Free: last 12 months. Full history: Futures Daily or Complete
Continuous series  | 131 markets since 2008  | Rolled on a published roll calendar; back-adjusted (difference method) or unadjusted  | Free: last 12 months. Full history: Futures Daily or Complete
Intraday bars  | 139 markets since February 2007  | Hourly, 30-minute, 5-minute and 1-minute bars  | Futures Complete, or one market
Daily bars (open, high, low, close, volume, open interest) cover 17,586 individual contracts since 2007, plus continuous back-adjusted series and a roll calendar. Prices: one market $19, Futures Daily (all 139 markets, daily bars) $95, Futures Complete (adds 1-minute, 5-minute, 30-minute and hourly bars) $295. The last 12 months of daily bars are free. Tick-by-tick trades, quotes and order-book depth are not offered. See ES, NQ, CL, GC and ZN.

### What historical futures data does FinzData have?

Daily bars for 139 futures markets and 17,586 individual contracts since 2007, intraday bars at 1-minute, 5-minute, 30-minute and hourly resolution since February 2007, a roll calendar, and continuous series for 131 markets since 2008.

### What is back-adjusted continuous futures data?

A continuous series follows the contract in use each day. Back-adjusted prices shift every bar before a roll by the gap between the new and old contract on the roll day, so the series has no artificial jumps and the latest prices equal the live contract. Use adjust=none for raw prices.

### Can I download 1-minute futures data?

Yes. 1-minute, 5-minute, 30-minute and hourly bars come with Futures Complete ($295, all 139 markets) or a one-market purchase ($19).

### How do I download futures data as CSV?

Every API route returns JSON, CSV or Parquet: add format=csv, for example /v1/futures/daily?root=ES&continuous=true&format=csv. The Python client returns a pandas DataFrame.

### Is there free historical futures data?

Yes. The free API key includes the last 12 months of daily bars for all 139 futures markets.

### What time zone are intraday futures bars in?

Timestamps mark the start of each bar in US Eastern time, the same convention as FinzData equity bars.
